scenes.narration: Strip Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Either/Or (Danish: Enten – Eller) is the first published work of Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard. It appeared in two volumes in 1843 under the pseudonymous editorship of Victor Eremita (Latin for "victorious hermit").

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) shows exactly where that breaks. It outlines a theory of human existence, marked by the distinction between an essentially hedonistic, aesthetic mode of life and the ethical life, which is predicated upon commitment. Each life view is written and represented by a fictional author, with the prose reflecting and depending on the life view.

What looks like free choice in Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) is older than choice itself. The aesthetic life view is written in short essay form, with poetic imagery and allusions, discussing aesthetic topics such as music, seduction, drama, and beauty. The ethical life view is written as two long letters, with a more argumentative and restrained prose, discussing moral responsibility, critical reflection, and marriage.

Nobody designed the part of Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) you experience — it was inherited. The aesthetic is the personal, subjective realm of existence, where an individual lives and extracts pleasure from life for its own sake. The ethical, on the other hand, is the civic realm of existence, where value and identity are judged and at times superseded by the objective world.

Every serious account of Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. The choice is whether to remain oblivious to the outside world or to become involved. More specifically, the ethical realm starts with a conscious effort to choose one's life.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Either way it is possible to go too far in one direction and lose sight of the self. Either/Or concludes with a brief sermon hinting at the religious sphere of existence, which consumed most of Kierkegaard's publishing career.

The selfish-gene reading of Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) makes it less romantic and far more precise. Ultimately, his challenge is for the reader to "discover a second face hidden behind the one you see" internally, and then in others. After writing and defending his dissertation On the Concept of Irony with Continual Reference to Socrates (1841), Kierkegaard left Copenhagen in October 1841 to spend the winter in Berlin.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. His main purpose was to attend lectures by German philosopher Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, an eminent figure at the time. The lectures disappointed many in Schelling's audience, including Mikhail Bakunin and Friedrich Engels, while Kierkegaard described it as "unbearable nonsense".

The feeling that Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. During his stay, Kierkegaard worked on the manuscript for Either/Or, took daily lessons to perfect his German, and attended operas and plays, particularly by Mozart and Goethe. He returned to Copenhagen in March 1842 with a draft of the manuscript, which he completed late that year and published in February 1843.

Nothing in Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) was built for you — it was built for reproduction. According to a journal entry from 1846, Either/Or was written "lock, stock, and barrel in eleven months" ("Rub og Stub, i 11 Maaneder"), although a page from the "Diapsalmata" section in the "A" volume was written earlier. The title Either/Or affirmed Aristotelian logic, particularly as modified by Johann Gottlieb Fichte and Immanuel Kant.

The psychology underneath Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) is simpler and older than the story on top. Is the question, "Who am I?" a scientific question or one for the individual to answer? Kierkegaard argues that Hegel's philosophy dehumanized life by denying personal freedom and choice through the neutralization of the "either/or".

Behind Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. The dialectic structure of becoming renders existence far too easy, in Hegel's theory, because conflicts are eventually mediated and disappear through a natural process that requires no individual choice other than a submission to the Will of the Idea or Geist. Kierkegaard saw this as a denial of selfhood and instead advocated the importance of personal responsibility and choice.

The nihilist does not deny Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) — he only refuses to flatter it. The book is the first of Kierkegaard's works written pseudonymously, a practice he employed during the first half of his career. Kierkegaard published the second edition of Either/Or on May 14, 1849, the same day he published The Lily of the Field and the Bird of the Air: Three Devotional Discourses.

What culture calls destiny in Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. It contains a collection of papers, notionally found by "Victor Eremita" and written by "A", the aesthete. The aesthete, according to Kierkegaard, eventually falls into despair, a psychological state (explored further in Kierkegaard's The Concept of Anxiety and The Sickness Unto Death) that results from a recognition of the limits of the aesthetic approach to life.

The genes do not care about Either/Or (Kierkegaard book); they care about copies. The natural reaction is to make an eventual leap to the second phase, the ethical, which is characterized by rational choice and commitment that replace the capricious and inconsistent longings of the aesthetic mode. The first section of Part I is a collection of tangential aphorisms, epigrams, anecdotes, and musings on the aesthetic mode.

Take away the meaning and Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) still functions — that is the disturbing part. It contains some of Kierkegaard's best-known and poetic lines, such as "What is a poet?", "Freedom of Speech" vs. "Freedom of Thought", the "Unmovable chess piece", the tragic clown, and the laughter of the gods. Reading these as written shows a constant movement from the outer poetic experience to the inner experience of humor.

The unconscious does not argue with Either/Or (Kierkegaard book); it simply acts first. The movement from the outer to the inner is a theme in Kierkegaard's works. He becomes lost in the multiplicity of the "1,003 women he has to seduce" (as in the famous aria "Madamina, il catalogo è questo"), Faust seduces just one woman.

Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. This section deals with theological questions. "A" asks if God seduces 1,003 people at one time or if he seduces one individual at a time in order to make a believer. Arnim tells somewhere of a seducer of a very different style, a seducer who falls under ethical categories.

The bleak reading of Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) is also the most testable one. About him he uses an expression which in truth, boldness, and conciseness is almost equal to Mozart’s stroke of the bow. He says he could so talk with a woman that, if the devil caught him, he could wheedle himself out of it if he had a chance to talk with the devil’s grandmother.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Either/Or (Kierkegaard book). This is the real seducer; the aesthetic interest here is also different, namely: how, the method. The next three sections are essay lectures from "A" to the "symparanekromenoi", a club or fellowship of the dead who practice the art of writing posthumous papers.

The self that experiences Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) is a committee, not a king. The first essay, which discusses ancient and modern tragedy, is the "Ancient Tragical Motif as Reflected in the Modern". He also discusses guilt, sin, fear, compassion, and responsibility in what can be considered a foreshadowing of Fear and Trembling and Repetition.

Reproduction explains more of Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) than any philosophy dares to admit. The second essay, "Shadowgraphs: A Psychological Pastime", discusses modern heroines, including Mozart's Elvira and Goethe's Gretchen (Margaret). Psychologically he is asking whether psychologists can give an accurate account of the inner world.

Once you see Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Religiously he's asking whether one person can accurately perceive the inner world of another. The third essay, called "The Unhappiest One", discusses the hypothetical question: "who deserves the distinction of being unhappier than everyone else?" Kierkegaard has expanded his search for the highest to a search for the lowest.

The story Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Is it Niobe, Job, the father of the prodigal son, or Periander, Abraham or Christ? Ultimately, for Kierkegaard, the aesthetical and the ethical are both superseded by a final phase which he terms the "religious" mode.

Meaning is not found in Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) — it is manufactured for it. In this volume, Kierkegaard examines the concept of "First Love" as a pinnacle for the aesthete, using his concepts of "closedness" (indesluttethed in Danish) and "demonic" (demoniske) with reference to Eugène Scribe. Kierkegaard rejected any template in the field of literature or of Christianity.

The cold light on Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. He was against systematizing literature, because the system forces the artist to settle down within the system. He  considers how much of the muse's calling depends on the muse, how much on the individual, and how much on will/volition.

Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. Scribe's play is 16 pages long leading Kierkegaard to write a 50-page review. He attends a performance and sees his lover at a play called First Love; for him this is a sign, like a four-leaf clover, that she must be the one.

The honest version of Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) starts by giving up the comforting part. To Kierkegaard's aesthete, boredom is the root of all evil, and must be avoided. Boredom rests upon the nothing that interlaces existence; its dizziness is infinite, like that which comes from looking into a bottomless abyss.

Strip Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. He uses irony, artifice, caprice, imagination and arbitrariness to engineer poetically satisfying possibilities; he is not so much interested in the act of seduction as in willfully creating its interesting possibility. The Seducer is reminiscent of Faust Part 1, Scene VII (A Street).

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) shows exactly where that breaks. Faust says to Mephistopheles, "Listen, you must get that girl for me!" Mephistopheles says she's an "innocent" girl, but Faust says she's "older than 14". The Seducer knows the value of chance and wants to use chance to be "a possibility which seems an impossibility".

What looks like free choice in Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) is older than choice itself. Anyone who, when he is twenty years old, does not understand that there is a categorical imperative—Enjoy—is a fool, and anyone who does not start doing it is a Christiansfelder. .... Victor is a fanatic; Constantin has paid too much for his intellect; the Fashion Designer is a madman.

Nobody designed the part of Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) you experience — it was inherited. All four of you after the same girl will turn out to be a fizzle! Kierkegaard explores the category of choice and the aesthetic as well as the ethical.

Every serious account of Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Both can choose to love each other but the "how" of love is Kierkegaard's subject. Eremita found a group of letters from a retired Judge Vilhelm or William (in Danish: "Assessor Wilhelm"), another pseudonymous author, to "A", trying to convince "A" of the value of the ethical life by arguing that the ethical person can still appreciate aesthetic values.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Either/Or (Kierkegaard book) — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. The difference is that the pursuit of pleasure is tempered with ethical values and responsibilities.
